pages.text: It was the week of Hogbetsotso, the festival the Anlo celebrate on the first Sunday of November. Drums sounded in the distance. Worlanyo and Ayele sat beside Grandfather Dotse under the tree. “Grandfather,” said Ayele, “this festival remembers a journey. Please tell us how our people came here.”
sentences: It was the week of Hogbetsotso, the festival the Anlo celebrate on the first Sunday of November.
Drums sounded in the distance.
Worlanyo and Ayele sat beside Grandfather Dotse under the tree.
“Grandfather,” said Ayele, “this festival remembers a journey.
Please tell us how our people came here.”
pages.alt: Two children sit beside their grandfather under a tree while drums are heard in the distance.

pages.text: “Long ago,” said Grandfather, “many Ewe people lived in a walled town called Notsé, in what is now Togo. Its ruler was called Agokoli, or Agorkoli, because the spelling changes from book to book. The people say he ruled harshly, and that the wall around the town became a prison.”
sentences: “Long ago,” said Grandfather, “many Ewe people lived in a walled town called Notsé, in what is now Togo.
Its ruler was called Agokoli, or Agorkoli, because the spelling changes from book to book.
The people say he ruled harshly, and that the wall around the town became a prison.”
pages.alt: An old walled town with a tall mud wall and a ruler on a stool.

pages.text: “The people wanted to leave,” said Grandfather, “but the wall was thick and guarded. So the story says the women poured their washing water in the same place on the wall, again and again. Slowly the mud grew soft. At last a gap opened, and the people slipped out into the night.”
sentences: “The people wanted to leave,” said Grandfather, “but the wall was thick and guarded.
So the story says the women poured their washing water in the same place on the wall, again and again.
Slowly the mud grew soft.
At last a gap opened, and the people slipped out into the night.”
pages.alt: Women pour water at one spot on a tall mud wall as the sky grows dark.

pages.text: “There was one more trick,” said Grandfather. “To confuse anyone who followed, they walked backwards. Their footprints seemed to lead into the town, not away from it.” Ayele laughed. “That is clever!” “That is the tradition,” said Grandfather gently. “Now ask me what the historians say.”
sentences: “There was one more trick,” said Grandfather.
“To confuse anyone who followed, they walked backwards.
Their footprints seemed to lead into the town, not away from it.” Ayele laughed.
“That is clever!” “That is the tradition,” said Grandfather gently.
“Now ask me what the historians say.”
pages.alt: Footprints in sand appear to point towards a town while people walk away backwards.

pages.text: “Archaeologists have studied the remains at Notsé,” said Grandfather. “They think the great enclosure was a sacred and symbolic wall, not a fort. Some historians doubt the part about breaking through it, because the wall may never have been finished. But almost everyone agrees that a large movement of people from Notsé really happened.”

“They think the great enclosure was a sacred and symbolic wall, not a fort.
Some historians doubt the part about breaking through it, because the wall may never have been finished.
But almost everyone agrees that a large movement of people from Notsé really happened.”
pages.alt: A pair of archaeologists measure the remains of an old wall in a field.

pages.text: “And when did it happen?” asked Worlanyo. “Books do not agree,” said Grandfather. “Some put it in the fifteenth century, others in the sixteenth or the seventeenth. One writer gives Agokoli’s reign as 1670 to 1720. We say: dates uncertain, event likely.” Worlanyo wrote that down carefully, with a question mark.

We say: dates uncertain, event likely.” Worlanyo wrote that down carefully, with a question mark.
pages.alt: A notebook page with three centuries listed and a question mark beside them.

pages.text: “After they left, the people split into groups,” said Grandfather. “Some went north and west, to places like Hohoe, Kpando and Peki. Some settled near Ho. Others went south and west to the coast. The Anlo settled along the sea.” Ayele traced the route on a map with her finger. “That is how a single story became many towns.”

Some settled near Ho.
Others went south and west to the coast.
The Anlo settled along the sea.” Ayele traced the route on a map with her finger.
“That is how a single story became many towns.”
pages.alt: A map of the Volta Region with arrows leaving Notsé towards different towns.

pages.text: “So is Notsé where the Ewe began?” asked Ayele. “Many Ewe say so,” said Grandfather. “Historians say the Ewe lived in this region before Notsé, so it may be a story of a great journey and not the very first beginning. Both can be true. A people can remember a moment that made them who they are.” The drums grew louder. “Come. The festival is starting.” The end.

A people can remember a moment that made them who they are.” The drums grew louder.
“Come.
The festival is starting.” The end.
